text: This chapter is the capstone — one real business process, built across three lessons, pulling together every mechanism this course has taught so far instead of practicing them one at a time in isolation.

The scenario is Contractor Offboarding at a mid-size company. Contractors live on a table with an end date, a contractor type, and a manager. When a contractor's end date arrives, three things need to happen: their system access gets revoked, their manager confirms equipment was returned, and IT gets a task to actually disable the account. Right now, all three only happen if someone remembers to do them by hand — which is exactly the kind of manual, inconsistent process Flow Designer exists to replace.

A Record trigger fires the instant a record is inserted or updated — it's built for events. But the end date field was set weeks earlier, when the contractor was onboarded, and nothing changes on that record on the day it actually matters. That's a Scheduled trigger problem instead: run daily, early in the morning, and query for contractors whose end date is today and who are still marked active. The trigger's query does the finding; the flow does the acting.

Before opening Flow Designer, sketch the flow in plain steps. A scheduled trigger finds today's contractors. An If/Else branches on contractor type, since IT and non-IT contractors have different systems to revoke access from. Revoking access works the same way no matter which branch got there — a strong sign it belongs in a reusable subflow rather than inline logic. A manager approval confirms equipment return before the flow continues. And a concrete, assigned IT task makes disabling the account someone's actual responsibility, not just a notification that could be ignored.

That five-step sketch is the plan, written in plain language before a single node gets dragged onto the canvas. Next, you'll actually build it in Flow Designer — the branch, the subflow call, the approval, and the task — in Lesson 26.
